title: UpKeep Alternative for Small Maintenance Teams (2026)
summary: Compare UpKeep vs Taskade Genesis for small maintenance teams. Own work orders, PM intervals, and asset history without CMMS seat tax or parts-module bloat.
body_text: Blog AI UpKeep Alternative for Small… On this page (19) UpKeep helped thousands of facilities teams leave clipboards and shared inboxes. For a five-person maintenance shop, the same product can feel like renting a factory floor when you only needed a clean work-order board. This guide is the honest 2026 path for small shops comparing UpKeep, MaintainX, Limble, Maintoro, and a living ops board you own in Taskade Genesis . TL;DR: Packaged CMMS tools win when you need inventory modules, meter APIs, and a vendor-shaped mobile CMMS day one. Taskade Genesis wins when you want work orders, PM intervals, and customer context in a living app you reshape. Start from the UpKeep alternative work order board , pair a MaintainX-style PM board if intervals matter, and keep GPS, payroll, and parts warehouse tools beside the board instead of inventing them inside it. Pricing below uses publicly listed or widely reported 2026 ranges (annual billing where vendors publish it). Confirm live quotes before you buy. Vendors change tiers. 🧰 What Small Shops Actually Need From a CMMS A full computerized maintenance management system promises assets, work orders, preventive maintenance, parts, purchasing, meters, and reports. Small shops usually live in a narrower week: Someone reports a broken unit (text, email, or walk-up). A lead triages priority and assigns a tech. The tech closes the job with notes, photos, and time spent. Someone schedules the next PM before the same unit fails again. An owner wants a board that answers "what is open?" without hunting chat threads. That spine is an ops board. It is not the same as a warehouse CMMS. Confusing the two is how shops overbuy seats. Daily need Packaged CMMS default Living ops board in Taskade Genesis Open work orders Native WO module Project board with status columns Asset list Asset registry Linked asset records in Projects PM cadence PM scheduler (often paid tier) Recurring tasks + automation reminders Parts bin levels Inventory module (often Premium+) Pair your inventory tool; the board is not a warehouse Fleet GPS Vendor or partner add-on Not available. Keep your telematics Who configures fields Vendor templates You + Taskade EVE chat If your week is the five steps above, you are shopping for ownership of the board. If your week is cycle counts, PO approvals, and meter-driven reorder points, stay in a dedicated CMMS. 📜 Origin of the CMMS Seat-Tax Problem CMMS pricing grew up around plants and multi-site facilities teams. Per-user licensing made sense when every technician needed a licensed login, and when the vendor funded a deep mobile app, barcode scanning, and inventory ledgers. Then three things changed for small shops: Everyone became a requester. Front desk, tenants, and machine operators submit work. Vendors responded with free requester seats, which is good, but paid "full users" still stack when leads, techs, and managers all need write access. Chat and spreadsheets became the real system of record. Many shops already coordinate in SMS and Sheets. Buying a CMMS seat for each person who occasionally updates a status feels like a tax on visibility. AI and app builders collapsed the cost of a custom board. In 2026 you can generate a work-order app from a prompt, then reshape fields without filing a ticket. That shifts the buy decision from "which CMMS brand?" to "do we rent a schema or own one?" The seat tax is not a moral failure by UpKeep or MaintainX. It is a business model matched to packaged depth. Small shops feel it when Essential pricing is fine for three people and painful at twelve, or when the features they need (PM, inventory, offline) live one tier up. That loop is what Taskade Genesis is built to own. Parts warehouses and GPS trails are adjacent systems. 💵 2026 Pricing Reality: UpKeep, MaintainX, Limble, Maintoro Use this as a budget sketch, not a contract. Figures are approximate public ranges as of mid-2026. Product Entry / free Practical paid start Next tier often needed Notes for small shops UpKeep Trial, then paid Essential ~$20-$24/user/mo Premium ~$55/user/mo Essential covers core WOs; PM and inventory often push Premium MaintainX Free Basic (limits) Essential $20/user/mo annual ($25 monthly) Premium $65/user/mo annual ($75 monthly) Free is real for light use; Premium is where inventory/API depth lands Limble Quote / calculator Standard ~$28/user/mo annual (reports vary ~$28-$35) Premium+ ~$55-$69/user/mo Strong CMMS depth; pricing less list-page transparent Maintoro Free (tight limits, e.g. 2 users) Starter ~$15/user/mo annual Pro ~$39/user/mo annual Lower seat price; still a CMMS product shape Taskade Genesis Free plan available Workspace plans (not CMMS per-tech seats) Higher plans for more AI/app users Own the ops board; pair inventory/GPS elsewhere Rough monthly seat math (paid users only) Paid users UpKeep Essential (~$22 avg) MaintainX Essential (~$20) Limble Standard (~$28) Maintoro Starter (~$15) 3 ~$66 ~$60 ~$84 ~$45 5 ~$110 ~$100 ~$140 ~$75 10 ~$220 ~$200 ~$280 ~$150 15 ~$330 ~$300 ~$420 ~$225 Bump those numbers if you need Premium-class inventory or offline. A ten-person MaintainX Premium line is ~$650/mo on annual Premium marketing rates, not ~$200. How Taskade Genesis changes the equation: you are not buying CMMS seats. You buy a workspace that holds Projects, Agents, and Automations, then invite the people who run the board. Published app end users and AI credit usage follow Taskade plan rules, which is a different meter than "every tech is a CMMS license." body_text: Genprex Selects Leading Clinical and Commercial Contract Development and Manufacturing Organization for Manufacturing Scale Up of Diabetes Gene Therapy August 18, 2026 Press Releases Diabetes gene therapy Collaboration Allows Genprex to Accelerate Manufacturing Processes for IND-Enabling Preclinical Studies and Future Clinical Trials AUSTIN, Texas — (Aug.18, 2026) — Genprex, Inc. (“Genprex” or the “Company”) (NASDAQ: GNPX ), a clinical-stage gene therapy company focused on developing life-changing therapies for patients with cancer and diabetes, today announced that it has entered into a development and manufacturing agreement with a leading U.S. based clinical and commercial Contract Development and Manufacturing Organization (CDMO) to initiate the manufacturing scale-up of its diabetes gene therapy program. This strategic selection allows for the transition of the Company’s therapeutic candidate from research-grade production to clinical and commercial-ready output. This collaboration provides the infrastructure necessary to produce the Company’s AAV-based therapy in a current Good Manufacturing Practices (cGMP) compliant facility. The CDMO will manufacture and supply drug product to be used in Genprex’s IND-enabling preclinical studies and future clinical trials. “This strategic partnership represents a significant advancement for our diabetes gene therapy clinical program,” said Ryan Confer, President and Chief Executive Officer at Genprex. “We have transferred the manufacturing process for our diabetes product candidate from the academic setting, where it was previously manufactured, into a reputable cGMP compliant CDMO. Through this collaboration, Genprex aims to advance its diabetes gene therapy program toward clinical evaluation, focusing on the safety and efficacy required for upcoming toxicology studies.” By partnering with an established CDMO, the Company gains access to specialized expertise in scaling complex biologics, ensuring consistent delivery of the therapeutic payload, a critical factor for administration in patients with Type 1 diabetes (T1D) and Type 2 diabetes (T2D). The manufacturing roadmap includes several technical priorities: Process Optimization: Using latest AAV production technologies to increase production efficiency. Scale Up: Use of capacity bioreactors to increase dose availability in preparation for multi-center trials. Analytical Qualification and Development of Potency Assay: Implementing rigorous quality control protocols to ensure AAV potency, stability and purity. GMP Compliance: Maintaining strict adherence to cGMP standards to support future regulatory submissions. Genprex’s diabetes gene therapy product candidate involves the delivery of the Pdx1 and MafA genes into the pancreas via the pancreatic duct utilizing an AAV vector. Novel advanced technologies were incorporated in these processes to optimize the plasmid construct to increase stability of expression and modify the backbone to align with other plasmids used for AAV products. The new plasmid was cloned, purified, and manufactured and is currently being used in the manufacture of AAV. Genprex is continuing work with CDMOs and research partners to optimize constructs and evaluate alternative second-generation approaches including different AAV and non-viral constructs. The Company’s strategic collaboration with a CDMO to research a non-viral lipid nanoparticle delivery of its diabetes gene therapy drug candidate could allow for potential re-dosing of patients to optimize treatment. Genprex’s diabetes gene therapy product candidate is under development as a potential treatment for both T1D and T2D. In T1D, the drug candidate is designed to work by transforming alpha cells in the pancreas into functional beta-like cells, which can produce insulin but may be distinct enough from beta cells to evade the body’s immune system. In vivo, preclinical studies show that the drug candidate restored normal blood glucose levels for an extended period of time in T1D mouse models. In T1D NHP in vivo models, the drug candidate demonstrated the ability to decrease insulin requirements, increase c-peptide levels and improve glucose tolerance. In a similar approach for T2D, where autoimmunity is not at play, the drug candidate demonstrated the ability to replenish and rejuvenate exhausted beta cells that make insulin in both mouse and NHP models. About Genprex, Inc. Genprex, Inc. is a clinical-stage gene therapy company focused on developing life-changing therapies for patients with cancer and diabetes. Genprex’s technologies are designed to administer disease-fighting genes to provide new therapies for large patient populations with cancer and diabetes who currently have limited treatment options. Genprex works with world-class institutions and collaborators to develop drug candidates to further its pipeline of gene therapies in order to provide novel treatment approaches. Genprex’s oncology program utilizes its systemic, non-viral Oncoprex® Delivery System which encapsulates the gene-expressing plasmids using lipid-based nanoparticles in a lipoplex form. The resultant product is administered intravenously, where it is taken up by tumor cells that then express tumor suppressor proteins that were deficient in the tumor. The Company’s lead product candidate, Reqorsa® Gene Therapy (quaratusugene ozeplasmid), is being evaluated in two clinical trials as a treatment for NSCLC and SCLC. Each of Genprex’s lung cancer clinical programs has received a Fast Track Designation from the FDA for the treatment of that patient population, and Genprex’s SCLC program has received an FDA Orphan Drug Designation. Genprex’s diabetes gene therapy approach is comprised of a novel infusion process that uses an AAV vector to deliver Pdx1 and MafA genes directly to the pancreas. In models of Type 1 diabetes, GPX-002 transforms alpha cells in the pancreas into functional beta-like cells, which can produce insulin but may be distinct enough from beta cells to evade the body’s immune system. In a similar approach for Type 2 diabetes, where autoimmunity is not at play, GPX-002 is believed to rejuvenate and replenish exhausted beta cells. title: Cloud Data Center: Definition and Model
summary: Turbocharge the way you order custom parts with our instant quoting engine. Get DFM feedback, lead times, and pricing in a matter of clicks, not days.
body_text: A cloud data center is a large-scale facility that delivers computing resources, storage capacity, and networking services to organizations through internet-connected infrastructure. Cloud computing data center operations replace the need for on-premises hardware by hosting virtualized workloads across shared physical servers managed by third-party providers. The article covers the definition, key components, models, architecture layers, cost structure, and real-world applications of cloud data center deployments. Cloud infrastructure data center environments span public, private, hybrid, and virtual models, structured to meet distinct performance, compliance, and cost requirements. Cloud data center facilities house tens of thousands to more than 1,000,000 physical servers, depending on provider scale and geographic footprint. AWS, Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud operate hundreds of cloud data center sites across 30 to 40 global regions. Power draw per hyperscale cloud facility ranges from 20 MW to more than 100 MW, with PUE ratings from 1.1 to 1.4 across leading operators. Cooling, power redundancy, physical security, and network connectivity form four infrastructure pillars supporting continuous cloud service delivery at 99.99% to 99.999% availability targets across enterprise-grade agreements. What Is a Cloud Data Center? A cloud data center is a purpose-built facility that houses the physical hardware servers, storage arrays, networking equipment, and power systems required to deliver on-demand computing services over the internet to multiple simultaneous tenants. The facility abstracts physical hardware into virtualized resource pools, allowing organizations to consume compute, storage, and network capacity without owning or managing the underlying equipment. Cloud data centers differ from traditional enterprise data centers in ownership model, billing structure, and scalability, with cloud facilities charging per-unit consumption rather than requiring capital investment in physical hardware. A single hyperscale cloud data center campus spans from 100,000 to over 1,000,000 square feet of conditioned floor space, housing server counts from 50,000 to over 500,000 nodes per site. Virtualization platforms (VMware vSphere, Microsoft Hyper-V, KVM) partition physical server resources into isolated virtual machines, enabling resource-sharing across thousands of concurrent tenants without performance interference. Network fabric within the facility connects compute and storage nodes through spine-and-leaf switching architectures at bandwidths from 10 Gbps to 400 Gbps per server port. Power infrastructure follows 2N redundancy configurations, ensuring no single electrical failure interrupts active workloads. Cooling systems maintain server inlet temperatures from 15°C to 32°C per ASHRAE A1 specifications across the facility floor. The geographic distribution of cloud data center campuses across multiple regions and availability zones provides fault isolation, disaster recovery, and latency reduction for globally distributed application workloads. What Are the Key Components of a Cloud Data Center? The key components of a cloud data center include physical and virtual systems providing compute, storage, networking, power, cooling, security, and virtualization services across cloud computing environments. Each component performs a specific function supporting resource availability, workload delivery, and continuous service operation. The key components of a cloud data center are listed below. Servers: Servers execute virtualized workloads, process application requests, and host multiple virtual machines on shared physical hardware. Enterprise cloud servers support from 20 to over 100 virtual machines per physical server, depending on hardware capacity and workload requirements. Storage Systems: Storage systems retain and deliver tenant data through block, file, and object storage architectures connected to compute nodes. Flash-based storage arrays support high input/output performance, while object storage platforms scale across distributed storage clusters. Network Equipment: Network equipment connects servers, storage systems, and external networks through switches, routers, and load balancers. Software-defined networking (SDN) enables programmable network management and automated traffic control across cloud environments. Power Systems: Power systems supply conditioned electrical power through redundant Uninterruptible Power Supply (UPS), Power Distribution Unit (PDU), and generator systems. Redundant power paths maintain continuous operation during electrical failures and scheduled maintenance. Cooling Systems: Cooling systems remove heat generated by servers and networking equipment through air cooling, liquid cooling, and immersion cooling methods. High-density cloud deployments use advanced cooling technologies to maintain stable operating temperatures. Security Systems: Security systems protect cloud data centers through physical access controls, surveillance, encryption, and network security technologies. Layered security measures safeguard facilities, hardware, and tenant data against unauthorized access. Virtualization Layer: The virtualization layer divides physical compute, storage, and networking resources into isolated virtual environments using hypervisor software. Virtualization enables efficient resource allocation, workload isolation, and rapid provisioning across cloud platforms. What Role Does a Server Rack Play in a Cloud Data Center? A server rack in a cloud data center is the standardized physical enclosure that mounts, organizes, and connects servers, storage nodes, networking hardware, and power distribution units into a single manageable vertical unit within the facility floor. Server racks in cloud environments follow the ECA 310-D standard, measuring 42U in height, 600 mm to 800 mm in width, and 1,000 mm to 1,200 mm in depth, with each rack unit (U) measuring 44.45 mm in height. Rack density in cloud data centers ranges from 5 kW to 20 kW per rack in standard air-cooled deployments, rising to 40 kW to 100 kW per rack in direct liquid-cooled configurations supporting GPU compute clusters. Cooling at the rack level takes the form of rear-door heat exchangers, in-row cooling units, and direct liquid cooling manifolds mounted within or adjacent to the rack enclosure, capturing server exhaust heat before it raises room air temperature. High-density racks in GPU cloud deployments carry load ratings from 1,500 kg to 2,000 kg to accommodate heavier liquid-cooled server chassis and coolant distribution hardware. Open-frame racks support unrestricted airflow access, while enclosed cabinets provide physical security with perforated door panels maintaining 60% to 80% open area for airflow continuity. Power distribution within the rack routes from dual PDUs fed by independent power circuits, following N+1 or 2N redundancy to prevent rack-level power loss from a single PDU failure. Cable management arms, vertical cable organizers, and horizontal patch panels within the rack maintain structured cabling pathways that reduce airflow obstruction and support rapid hardware swap operations. The physical density, cooling method, and power feed configuration of the server rack determine the compute capacity and availability profile of each rack position within the cloud facility. What Is Data Center Networking in a Cloud Environment? Data center networking in a cloud environment is the physical and virtual interconnect layer that links compute nodes, storage arrays, and external internet connections into a unified, programmable traffic management fabric operating across the facility. Networking in a cloud data center combines physical switching and routing hardware with SDN software that abstracts network topology into API-configurable virtual overlays, allowing tenant networks creation, modification, and deletion without physical reconfiguration. Switches form the foundational physical layer, connecting servers and storage nodes within the same network segment at speeds from 25 Gbps to 400 Gbps per port across spine-and-leaf topologies deployed in hyperscale cloud facilities. Spine switches aggregate traffic from multiple leaf switches, with hyperscale spine layers carrying aggregate bandwidths from 12.8 Tbps to 102.4 Tbps per spine switch chassis in high-density deployments. Load balancers distribute incoming application traffic across server pools using algorithms (round-robin, least connections, consistent hashing) at throughput rates from 10 Gbps to 1 Tbps per appliance, preventing overload on any single compute node. Virtual networks (VLANs, VXLANs) segment tenant traffic across shared physical switching infrastructure, with VXLAN supporting up to 16,777,216 isolated virtual network identifiers compared to 4,094 in standard VLAN implementations. Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) governs external routing from the cloud facility to internet exchange points, with cloud providers peering at over 100 internet exchange locations globally to minimize latency for end users. Network latency within the facility fabric measures below 1 ms for east-west traffic from compute to storage, while north-south latency to the internet depends on geographic distance from the nearest cloud region. The physical switching, SDN overlay, and traffic distribution architecture that forms data center networking determines the throughput, latency, and fault tolerance of every cloud workload running within the facility. What Is Data Center Storage in Cloud Infrastructure? Data center storage in cloud infrastructure is the physical and software-defined layer that retains, organizes, and serves structured and unstructured tenant data across block, file, and object storage architectures connected to compute nodes through dedicated high-speed storage networks. Block storage systems attach directly to virtual machines through iSCSI or Fibre Channel protocols, delivering latencies below 1 ms and IOPS counts from 3,000 to over 1,000,000 per volume, depending on storage tier and media type. File storage systems serve shared directory structures to multiple compute nodes simultaneously through NFS or SMB protocols, with throughput rates from 1 Gbps to 100 Gbps per storage controller depending on workload and network port configuration. Object storage platforms store unstructured data (images, video, backups, logs) across distributed storage nodes with no capacity ceiling, scaling from terabytes to exabytes without architectural changes to the storage system. Flash-based NVMe storage arrays deliver read latencies below 0.1 ms and sustained write throughput from 10 GB/s to over 100 GB/s per controller in high-performance cloud storage tiers. Storage redundancy in cloud environments follows erasure coding and replication schemes, with 3-way replication across geographically separated availability zones protecting against single-site data loss events. Storage Area Networks (SANs) within the facility interconnect dedicated storage arrays to server nodes through high-speed FC or iSCSI fabrics, isolating storage traffic from general network congestion on the compute switching fabric. Cloud storage pricing follows tiered consumption models, with hot storage tiers costing from [$0.02 to $0.08] per GB per month and cold archival tiers priced from [$0.001 to $0.004] per GB per month across major cloud providers. The block, file, and object layers of Data Center Storage collectively determine the performance, durability, and cost profile of tenant data retention across the cloud infrastructure. Does a Cloud Data Center Include Built-In Security Measures? Yes, a cloud data center includes built-in security measures across physical, network, and data layers that protect tenant workloads, stored data, and facility hardware from unauthorized access, interception, and physical threats. Physical security systems deploy biometric access controls, mantrap entry chambers, 24-hour closed-circuit surveillance, and security personnel at every facility entry point, restricting hardware access to verified personnel with documented authorization. Encryption standards protect tenant data at rest using AES-256 across storage arrays and in transit using TLS 1.3 across all network paths from tenant systems to cloud endpoints. Network security appliances firewalls, intrusion detection systems (IDS), and distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) mitigation platforms filter and inspect traffic entering and leaving the facility at throughput rates from 100 Gbps to over 10 Tbps per mitigation cluster. Access control systems enforce role-based permissions across tenant environments, restricting API access, virtual machine management, and storage operations to authenticated identities verified through multi-factor authentication (MFA). Compliance frameworks (SOC 2 Type II, ISO 27001, PCI DSS, HIPAA) govern security control implementation across cloud facilities, with third-party audits validating control effectiveness on annual or biannual cycles. Physical hardware destruction protocols govern the end-of-life processing of storage media, with DoD 5220.22-M or NIST SP 800-88 Rev. 1 erasure standards applied before drive decommissioning. Network segmentation through virtual private cloud (VPC) configurations isolates tenant traffic at the software-defined networking layer, preventing cross-tenant data access across shared physical switching infrastructure. The layered physical, logical, and cryptographic controls embedded across the facility define the Data Center Security posture that cloud providers maintain on behalf of every hosted tenant. What Are the Different Cloud Data Center Models? The different cloud data center models are deployment and ownership configurations that determine how computing resources are provisioned, managed, and accessed by organizations. Each model differs in resource ownership, operational responsibility, scalability, security, and cost structure. The different cloud data center models are listed below. Public Cloud Data Center: A public cloud data center is a multi-tenant facility operated by a third-party provider that delivers shared compute, storage, and networking resources over the internet on a pay-as-you-go basis. Private Cloud Data Center: A private cloud data center is a single-tenant environment dedicated to one organization, providing cloud capabilities while maintaining greater control over hardware, security, and resource management. Hybrid Cloud Data Center: A hybrid cloud data center combines private cloud resources with one or more public cloud environments, allowing workloads and data to move between platforms based on business, performance, or compliance requirements. Virtual Data Center: A virtual data center is a software-defined environment that presents virtualized compute, storage, and networking resources as a single manageable infrastructure without requiring direct access to physical hardware. Colocation Data Center: A colocation data center is a third-party facility where organizations lease rack space, power, cooling, and network connectivity while owning and managing their own servers and networking equipment. What Is a Public Cloud Data Center? A public cloud data center is a large-scale, multi-tenant facility owned, operated, and maintained by a third-party cloud service provider that delivers on-demand compute, storage, and networking resources to organizations over the internet through a pay-per-use consumption model. Physical infrastructure within a public cloud data center—servers, storage arrays, switches, power systems, and cooling equipment is owned entirely by the provider and shared across thousands of simultaneous tenant organizations through virtualization and software-defined resource partitioning. Provider-managed hyperscale public cloud facilities house server counts exceeding 500,000 nodes per campus, with individual availability zones within a cloud region housing from 50,000 to 150,000 servers across multiple buildings. Compute resources in public cloud environments are available in predefined instance types ranging from 1 vCPU and 1 GB RAM entry configurations to 192 vCPU and 1,536 GB RAM high-memory instances, priced from [$0.01 to $32.00] per hour, depending on instance family, region, and commitment level. Storage in public cloud facilities spans object, block, and file tiers with per-gigabyte monthly costs from [$0.001 to $0.08], depending on performance tier and access frequency. Network capacity within public cloud regions reaches aggregate bandwidths of multiple terabits per second, with inter-region data transfer priced from [$0.01 to $0.09] per GB across provider networks. Public cloud facilities achieve availability targets from 99.9% to 99.999% per service tier, backed by financially binding service-level agreements (SLAs) specifying credit structures for downtime events. Geographic distribution across 30 to 40 global regions per major provider allows tenant workloads to deploy in proximity to end users, reducing round-trip latency to below 10 ms in most metropolitan markets. What Is a Virtual Data Center? A virtual data center is a software-defined abstraction of physical compute, storage, and network resources that delivers a fully manageable virtual infrastructure environment to tenant organizations without direct interaction with underlying physical hardware. The virtualization layer is implemented through hypervisors (VMware ESXi, KVM, Microsoft Hyper-V) running on bare-metal servers, partition physical CPU cores, RAM, and storage volumes into isolated virtual machines (VMs) allocatable through management APIs or web consoles. Resource pooling aggregates the physical capacity of multiple servers, storage arrays, and network devices into a unified logical pool from which virtual resources are drawn and assigned to tenant workloads on demand. A physical server in a virtual data center environment hosts from 20 to over 100 VMs, depending on workload CPU and RAM requirements, with oversubscription ratios from 4:1 to 10:1 applied to CPU resources in mixed workload environments. Storage virtualization layers (VMware vSAN, Ceph) pool local drives across multiple servers into distributed storage clusters presenting block or object interfaces to VMs without dedicated external storage hardware. Network virtualization through SDN overlays (VMware NSX, OpenStack Neutron) creates isolated virtual network segments for each tenant, with VXLAN encapsulation supporting up to 16,777,216 isolated network identifiers across shared physical switching infrastructure. Virtual data centers scale in increments as granular as 1 vCPU and 1 GB RAM, eliminating the minimum hardware procurement thresholds of physical infrastructure deployments. Provisioning time for new virtual resources in a managed virtual data center measures in seconds to minutes, compared to weeks to months for physical hardware procurement and installation cycles. What Is a Cloud-Based Data Center Hosting Model? A cloud-based data center hosting model is a service delivery structure in which physical data center infrastructure—compute, storage, networking, power, and cooling is owned and operated by a third-party provider and consumed by tenant organizations as a metered service accessed over the internet. The hosting model eliminates capital expenditure on physical hardware by replacing ownership with subscription or consumption-based billing tied to actual resource usage measured in compute hours, storage gigabytes, and network transfer volumes. Infrastructure-as-a-Service (IaaS) represents the foundational cloud hosting layer, providing raw virtual compute, storage, and network resources configurable by the tenant, with pricing from [$0.01 to $32.00] per compute hour across major providers. Platform-as-a-Service (PaaS) hosting abstracts the operating system and middleware layer, delivering managed runtime environments for application development and deployment without tenant responsibility for server patching or infrastructure management. Software-as-a-Service (SaaS) hosting delivers fully managed application environments where the provider owns and operates every infrastructure, platform, and application layer, with tenants accessing only the application interface through a web browser or API. Multi-tenant hosting models share physical hardware across thousands of tenant organizations through virtualization, reducing per-tenant infrastructure cost compared to dedicated single-tenant hosting configurations. Dedicated hosted models allocate specific physical servers to a single tenant within the provider's facility, eliminating multi-tenancy at the hardware layer while retaining provider management of power, cooling, and network infrastructure. Reserved and committed-use billing options reduce cloud hosting costs by 30% to 72% compared to on-demand pricing across major IaaS providers, in exchange for 1-year or 3-year usage commitments. How Does Cloud Data Center Architecture Work? Cloud data center architecture is the structured arrangement of physical hardware, virtualization software, networking, storage, and management systems that deliver scalable and fault-tolerant cloud services. Each architectural layer performs a specific function supporting resource allocation, workload execution, data storage, network communication, and service availability. The main layers of cloud data center architecture are listed below. Physical Layer: The physical layer consists of servers, storage systems, networking equipment, power systems, and cooling systems that provide the hardware foundation supporting cloud computing operations. Virtualization Layer: The virtualization layer uses hypervisor software to partition physical computing resources into isolated virtual machines and containers, allowing multiple workloads to share the same hardware while remaining logically separated. Networking Layer: The networking layer connects servers, storage systems, and external networks through switches, routers, load balancers, and software-defined networking technologies that manage data communication and tenant isolation. Storage Layer: The storage layer provides block, file, and object storage services that retain application data while supporting scalability, redundancy, data protection, and high availability across cloud environments. Orchestration and Management Layer: The orchestration and management layer automates resource provisioning, monitoring, scaling, and lifecycle management across compute, storage, and networking resources through centralized management platforms, completing the Data Center Architecture . What Are the Core Layers of Cloud Infrastructure Data Center Design? The core layers of cloud infrastructure data center design are the functional tiers that organize physical hardware, virtualization, networking, storage, security, and management systems into a structured cloud environment. Each layer performs a dedicated role supporting resource allocation, workload execution, service availability, and operational efficiency. The core layers of cloud infrastructure data center design are listed below. Physical Infrastructure Layer: The physical infrastructure layer encompasses the building, raised flooring, server racks, power distribution, cooling systems, and structured cabling that house and support active hardware. Standard raised floor plenums install from 300 mm to 1,000 mm above the structural slab, distributing conditioned airflow at rates from 0.5 m³/s to 2.5 m³/s per perforated tile. Load ratings per rack position range from 900 kg to 2,000 kg, depending on cooling method and hardware density. Compute Layer: The compute layer consists of physical servers and hypervisor software that partition hardware resources into virtual machines and containers serving tenant workloads. Dual-socket server nodes carry from 64 to 192 CPU cores and from 512 GB to 6 TB of RAM per chassis in high-density cloud configurations. Compute layer capacity scales through server addition without architectural changes to higher layers. Storage Layer: The storage layer aggregates block, file, and object storage capacity across dedicated arrays, distributed storage clusters, and NVMe server-attached media into unified storage pools. Object storage scales to exabyte capacity across distributed nodes without single-system capacity limits. Flash-based block storage delivers IOPS from 500,000 to over 10,000,000 per array in performance cloud tiers. Network Layer: The network layer connects compute and storage nodes through spine-and-leaf physical fabrics and software-defined networking (SDN) overlays, providing tenant network isolation and east-west traffic forwarding at latencies below 1 ms. Spine switches carry aggregate bandwidths from 12.8 Tbps to 102.4 Tbps per chassis in hyperscale deployments. Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) peering at internet exchange points governs external traffic routing from the facility to global end users. Security Layer: The security layer applies encryption, access control, network segmentation, and physical access restrictions across each layer, protecting tenant data and facility hardware from unauthorized access. AES-256 encryption protects data at rest across storage arrays, while TLS 1.3 secures data in transit across network paths. Compliance frameworks including SOC 2, ISO 27001, and PCI DSS govern security control implementation and audit cycles. Management and Orchestration Layer: The management layer automates provisioning, monitoring, scaling, and incident response across compute, storage, and network resources through DCIM and cloud orchestration platforms. DCIM systems aggregate sensor data from thousands of monitoring points across the facility into unified dashboards. Automated orchestration platforms, including Kubernetes and OpenStack, reduce manual intervention in resource allocation and fault recovery cycles throughout the Infrastructure Data Center . Can Cloud Data Center Architecture support multi-region deployment? Yes, cloud data center architecture supports multi-region deployment through a distributed facility model that places independent data center clusters across geographically separated locations, each operating as an autonomous availability zone within a broader cloud region. A cloud region consists of from 2 to 6 availability zones, with each zone housed in one or more physically separate data center buildings connected through dedicated low-latency fiber links carrying bandwidths from 100 Gbps to multiple terabits per second. Geographic separation from availability zone to availability zone ranges from 10 km to over 100 km within a single cloud region, providing fault isolation against localized power outages, natural disasters, and network disruptions without cross-zone latency exceeding 2 ms. Multi-region deployments distribute application workloads across 2 or more cloud regions in different countries or continents, reducing end-user latency to below 50 ms in most global markets by serving requests from the nearest active region. Data replication across regions uses asynchronous or synchronous methods, with synchronous replication maintaining zero recovery point objectives (RPO) for mission-critical data at the cost of cross-region write latency from 10 ms to 100 ms, depending on geographic distance. Global load balancing systems route end-user DNS requests to the nearest healthy cloud region, failing over to secondary regions within 30 to 60 seconds of detecting a primary region service degradation event. Compliance requirements in regulated industries (financial services, healthcare, government) restrict data residency to specific geographic regions, with cloud providers offering dedicated regional deployments in over 30 countries to meet data sovereignty mandates. Multi-region architecture adds network egress costs from [$0.01 to $0.09] per GB for cross-region data transfer, requiring cost modeling against latency and availability benefits during deployment planning. What Are the Types of Cloud Data Centers? The types of cloud data centers are the distinct deployment models that determine how computing resources, physical facilities, and cloud services are owned, managed, and accessed by organizations. Each type differs in ownership structure, resource allocation, scalability, and operational control. The main types of cloud data centers are listed below. Public Cloud Data Center: A public cloud data center is a multi-tenant facility owned and operated by a third-party cloud provider that delivers shared computing resources over the internet on a pay-as-you-go pricing model. Major providers operate hundreds of facilities across 30 to 40 global regions. Compute pricing ranges from [$0.01 to $32.00] per hour, depending on instance type and deployment region. Private Cloud Data Center: A private cloud data center is a dedicated facility providing cloud-based services to a single organization within a controlled environment. Private cloud deployments require hardware investments ranging from [$500,000 to $50,000,000] per facility. VMware vSphere, OpenStack, and Nutanix AHV function as private cloud management platforms. Hybrid Cloud Data Center: A hybrid cloud data center combines private infrastructure with public cloud services through dedicated network connections or encrypted tunnels, allowing workloads to move between environments based on performance, cost, or compliance requirements. AWS Direct Connect and Azure ExpressRoute provide dedicated bandwidths from 1 Gbps to 100 Gbps. Hybrid deployments reduce public cloud costs by retaining predictable workloads on privately owned resources. Colocation Data Center: A colocation data center is a third-party facility that leases rack space, power, cooling, and network connectivity to organizations that install and manage their own hardware. Rack leasing costs range from [$500 to $5,000] per rack each month, depending on power density and geographic location. Customers maintain ownership and administrative control of all deployed equipment. Edge Data Center: An edge data center is a compact facility deployed close to users or connected devices to minimize network latency for time-sensitive applications. Edge facilities typically contain from 5 to 50 racks with power capacities ranging from 100 kW to 1 MW per site. Common workloads include industrial IoT, autonomous systems, and real-time video processing requiring response times below 10 milliseconds. Hyperscale Data Center: A hyperscale data center is a large-scale facility exceeding 100,000 square feet that supports more than 5,000 servers and power capacities ranging from 20 MW to over 100 MW. Hyperscale facilities commonly follow Open Compute Project (OCP) hardware standards to reduce equipment costs through standardized server designs. AWS, Microsoft, Google, and Meta operate the largest hyperscale cloud environments worldwide. What Is the Difference Between a Data Center and Cloud Data Center? A traditional data center and a cloud data center differ across ownership model, cost structure, scalability, maintenance responsibility, and deployment speed, with each configuration suited to distinct operational and financial requirements. title: Manifold Welcomes Evan Whipple as Technical Program Manager, Accelerating Customer Integrations
body_text: Every technology platform makes a promise. At Manifold, ours is straightforward: bring every freight opportunity into one place, eliminate the portal chaos, and make sure carriers and brokers never miss a spot opportunity because it came through the wrong channel. But a promise is only as good as the infrastructure behind it; and that infrastructure lives in the integrations, the connections between Manifold and the bid shipper and broker bid boards, and TMS platforms that our customers depend on every day. Delivering on those connections at speed and with precision requires a rare combination: deep technical expertise, a genuine understanding of how freight systems work in the real world, and the discipline to get things done on time. Manifold is proud to welcome Evan Whipple to the team as our new Technical Program Manager, his vast experience at Convoy and Amazon check those boxes with spades. A Career Spent at the Intersection of Freight and Technology Evan’s path to Manifold was shaped by seven years working at the forefront of freight technology. He spent a formative chapter at Convoy, the Seattle-based digital freight brokerage that became one of the most technically ambitious companies the logistics industry has ever seen. Convoy attracted some of the sharpest engineering minds in the country, and it was there that Evan built his foundation in the complex, high-stakes world of freight integrations. It was also there that he first crossed paths with Manifold’s Co-Founder and CEO, Oliver Jones, and Co-Founder and CTO Andrew Huff; a connection that would eventually bring him to Manifold. After Convoy, Evan took his expertise to Amazon, where he continued sharpening his instincts for large-scale systems, technical program management, and the kind of rigorous execution that enterprise-level logistics demands. By the time he encountered Manifold, the product’s value was immediately clear to him. “After seven years in the freight tech space, the value proposition of a cleanly aggregated spot board was obvious the moment I saw the product,” Evan says. “I am excited to join Manifold because we’re building next-gen tech for the freight industry.” Technology That Gives Time Back What struck Evan most about Manifold wasn’t just the technical architecture; it was the philosophy behind it. In an industry full of platforms that demand more attention, more logins, and more screen time, Manifold is built to do the opposite. “Unlike a lot of other tech companies, one of the rare things about Manifold is that we are building technology that lets our customers actually spend less time in front of a screen and more time on the relationships that are the foundation of the trucking industry,” he explains. “In addition to making our customers more money, I like that we’re also making their lives less stressful by letting them focus on just one screen rather than trying to juggle a dozen open bid boards.” That perspective runs deep. For Evan, the goal isn’t just operational efficiency; it’s something more human than that. “The psychological benefit of helping people breathe a little easier at the end of the day and making their lives feel less hectic is powerful,” he says. “These are hard problems to solve, but I’m particularly happy to be working on them with such a densely talented group of kind people.” What This Means for Manifold Customers In his role as Technical Program Manager, Evan’s mandate is clear: own every customer integration from start to finish, and deliver them on time and with precision. That means managing connections to customer bid boards, both shippers and broker bid boards, and TMS platforms; the technical touchpoints that determine whether a carrier or a broker sees every available load or misses the ones that matter most. This focus also frees up our Customer Success team to do what they do best: deepening relationships, supporting growth, and making sure every Manifold customer is getting the full value of the platform. Evan takes the integration complexity off their plate entirely. For customers, the impact is direct: faster onboarding, fewer delays between signing up and seeing results, and a dedicated expert whose entire job is making sure the technical foundation of their Manifold experience is rock solid. A Familiar Face, Exactly Where He Belongs For Oliver Jones, bringing Evan onto the Manifold team feels less like a hire and more like a reunion. “Evan is a perfect fit for this role and for our team,” says Jones. “We had the chance to work alongside him at Convoy, and we saw firsthand what he’s capable of: technical excellence, a deep understanding of how freight systems connect, and an absolute commitment to getting things done right. Our customers’ integration needs will be met on time and with precision. So excited to have join us.” Trey Griggs, Chief Revenue Officer at Manifold, echoed that enthusiasm. “We are insanely focused on customer success, and a massive aspect of creating a great customer experience is ensuring Manifold customers are connected with all of their spot opportunities,” he says. “Evan has the right technology experience and understanding of the transportation industry to knock this role out of the park, and we couldn’t be more thrilled to have him on the team.” Welcome, Evan The freight industry moves fast, and the carriers and brokers who win are the ones who can move faster. Manifold exists to give them that edge, and Evan’s arrival means the technical foundation of that promise just got a lot stronger. We’re glad to have you, Evan. Let’s get to work. Ready to see how Manifold brings every freight opportunity into one place? Schedule a demo and see what it looks like in action. ‍

summary: Achieved $57.5 million in RYTELO ® (imetelstat) net product revenue in Q2 2026, an increase of 11% compared to Q1 2026 Reiterated 2026 RYTELO net product revenue and total operating expenses expected to be in the ranges of $220 million to $240 million, and $230 million to $240 million, respectively
body_text: Geron Corporation Reports Second Quarter 2026 Financial Results and Recent Business Highlights August 5, 2026 PDF Version Achieved $57.5 million in RYTELO ® (imetelstat) net product revenue in Q2 2026, an increase of 11% compared to Q1 2026 Reiterated 2026 RYTELO net product revenue and total operating expenses expected to be in the ranges of $220 million to $240 million, and $230 million to $240 million, respectively Ended Q2 2026 with cash, cash equivalents, restricted cash and marketable securities of $327 million Broadened leadership team with the appointment of Chinmaya Rath as Chief Business Officer Company to host conference call and webcast today, August 5, 2026, at 8:00 a.m. ET FOSTER CITY, Calif., Aug. 05, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Geron Corporation (Nasdaq: GERN), a commercial-stage biopharmaceutical company aiming to change lives by changing the course of blood cancer, today reported financial results for the second quarter of 2026 and recent business highlights. “We are executing a focused strategy to build a leading hematology company, which starts with bringing RYTELO to more eligible patients impacted by LR-MDS in the U.S. Our team delivered a third consecutive quarter of RYTELO demand growth, and in the first half of 2026, grew net revenue by 24% while decreasing total operating expenses by 4% compared to the same period last year,” said Harout Semerjian, President and Chief Executive Officer of Geron. “With an estimated 8,000 second-line LR-MDS patients in the U.S., we see a meaningful opportunity to continue growing demand for RYTELO in 2026 and beyond. We also have the opportunity to create additional long-term value by expanding access to RYTELO in other geographies, advancing our Phase 3 IMpactMF trial in relapsed/refractory myelofibrosis and pursuing strategic innovation to develop and commercialize new therapies for people living with blood cancers.” Recent Business Highlights Reported RYTELO net product revenue of $57.5 million in the second quarter of 2026. Grew RYTELO demand by 5% in the second quarter 2026, compared to the first quarter 2026. Increased ordering accounts by roughly 8% in the second quarter 2026 to approximately 1,575. Presented the first real-world evidence study of RYTELO in patients with lower-risk myelodysplastic syndromes (LR-MDS) at the European Hematology Association (EHA) 2026 Congress. The retrospective portion of the investigator-sponsored study, conducted at the Moffitt Cancer Center, reported safety and clinical efficacy of imetelstat in advanced, heavily transfusion-dependent patients with LR-MDS, including patients with extensive prior therapies and after luspatercept failure. The efficacy, safety and tolerability observed were generally consistent with findings from the Phase 3 IMerge trial in a broader patient population.1 Presented two abstracts studying imetelstat in relapsed/refractory myelofibrosis at the 2026 American Society of Clinical Oncology (ASCO) Annual Meeting, including an updated overall survival analysis from the Phase 2 IMbark trial compared with real-world data. Broadened the leadership team with the appointment of Chinmaya Rath as Chief Business Officer. Second Quarter 2026 Financial Results Cash and Marketable Securities As of June 30, 2026, Geron had approximately $326.9 million in cash, cash equivalents, restricted cash and marketable securities, compared to $341.0 million as of March 31, 2026, which provides the Company with cash for the foreseeable future. Net Loss For the three months ended June 30, 2026, the Company reported a net loss of $16.7 million, or $0.02 per share, compared to $16.4 million, or $0.02 per share, for the three months ended June 30, 2025. The increase in net loss is directly attributable to non-cash inventory-related expenses, which were partially offset by an increase in RYTELO net product revenue for the quarter. Revenues Total product revenue, net for the three months ended June 30, 2026, was $57.5 million, compared to $49.0 million for the three months ended June 30, 2025. Costs and Operating Expenses Total costs and operating expenses for the three months ended June 30, 2026, were $70.0 million, compared to $61.5 million for the three months ended June 30, 2025. The increase is primarily due to non-cash inventory-related expenses. Cost of goods sold was approximately $9.2 million for the three months ended June 30, 2026, compared to $1.2 million for the three months ended June 30, 2025, which consisted of costs to manufacture and distribute RYTELO. The increase is primarily due to non-cash inventory-related expenses. Research and development expenses for the three months ended June 30, 2026, were $22.0 million, compared to $21.7 million for the same period in 2025. The increase in research and development expenses was a result of investments in manufacturing and was partially offset by lower headcount costs from the workforce reduction in December 2025. Selling, general and administrative expenses for the three months ended June 30, 2026, were $38.9 million, compared to $38.6 million for the same period in 2025. We continue to invest in our RYTELO commercialization strategy while managing lower general and administrative expenses primarily due to a decrease in personnel expense as a result of the workforce reduction in December 2025. 2026 Financial Guidance For fiscal year 2026, the Company expects RYTELO net product revenue to be in the range of $220 million to $240 million. Geron also expects total operating expenses to be between $230 million and $240 million. Total operating expenses include non-cash items such as stock-based compensation expense, amortization of debt discounts and issuance costs, inventory write-offs, depreciation and amortization. Based on current operating plans and assumptions, the Company believes that its existing cash, cash equivalents, restricted cash and marketable securities, together with anticipated net revenues from U.S. sales of RYTELO, will be sufficient to fund projected operating requirements for the foreseeable future. Conference Call Geron will host a conference call at 8:00 a.m. ET on Wednesday, August 5, 2026, to discuss business updates and second quarter 2026 financial results. A live webcast of the conference call will be available on the “Investors & Media” page of the Company’s website at www.geron.com . A replay of the webcast will be archived and available on the Company's website. 1. Data presented at the European Hematology Association (EHA) 2026 Congress: Komrokji RS, et al. “ Real-world Outcomes of Imetelstat: Interrogating Safety, Efficacy and Predictors of Response in Heavily Pretreated Lower-Risk MDS Patients .” Poster PF670. June 11-14, 2026, Stockholm, Sweden. About RYTELO (imetelstat) RYTELO (imetelstat) is an oligonucleotide telomerase inhibitor approved in the U.S. for the treatment of adult patients with lower-risk myelodysplastic syndromes (LR-MDS) with transfusion-dependent anemia requiring four or more red blood cell units over eight weeks who have not responded to or have lost response to or are ineligible for erythropoiesis-stimulating agents (ESAs). It is indicated to be administered as an intravenous infusion over two hours every four weeks. In addition, RYTELO is approved in the European Union as a monotherapy for the treatment of adult patients with transfusion-dependent anemia due to very low, low or intermediate risk myelodysplastic syndromes without an isolated deletion 5q cytogenetic (non-del 5q) abnormality and who had an unsatisfactory response to or are ineligible for erythropoietin-based therapy. RYTELO is a first-in-class treatment that works by inhibiting telomerase enzymatic activity. Telomeres are protective caps at the end of chromosomes that naturally shorten each time a cell divides. In LR-MDS, abnormal bone marrow cells often express the enzyme telomerase, which rebuilds those telomeres, allowing for uncontrolled cell division. Developed and exclusively owned by Geron, RYTELO is the first and only telomerase inhibitor approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration and the European Commission. Please see RYTELO (imetelstat) full Prescribing Information, including Medication Guide, available at https://pi.geron.com/products/US/pi/rytelo_pi.pdf . About Geron Geron is a commercial-stage biopharmaceutical company aiming to change lives by changing the course of blood cancer. Our first-in-class telomerase inhibitor RYTELO® (imetelstat) is approved in the United States and the European Union for the treatment of certain adult patients with lower-risk myelodysplastic syndromes with transfusion dependent anemia. We are also conducting a pivotal Phase 3 clinical trial of imetelstat in JAK-inhibitor relapsed/refractory myelofibrosis, as well as studies in other hematologic malignancies. To learn more, visit www.geron.com or follow us on LinkedIn . title: Beyond the Buzz: How AI Is Making Spa Experiences More Human
summary: Insights from an ISPA iLearn Partner Perspectives webinar featuring Agilysys SVP of Product Strategy and CMO Frank Pitsikalis, Jeremy McCarthy of Leisure Alchemy, and Kelleye Martin of The Houstonian Hotel, Club & Spa. Artificial intelligence is becoming increasingly prominent in hospitality, leading many spa operators to ask a practical question: Will AI make hospitality less […]
body_text: BLOGS August 19, 2026 Insights from an ISPA iLearn Partner Perspectives webinar featuring Agilysys SVP of Product Strategy and CMO Frank Pitsikalis , Jeremy McCarthy of Leisure Alchemy, and Kelleye Martin of The Houstonian Hotel, Club & Spa. Artificial intelligence is becoming increasingly prominent in hospitality, leading many spa operators to ask a practical question: Will AI make hospitality less personal? During a recent ISPA iLearn Partner Perspectives webinar, Agilysys SVP of Product Strategy and CMO Frank Pitsikalis joined Leisure Alchemy Principal Jeremy McCarthy and The Houstonian Hotel, Club & Spa Spa Director Kelleye Martin to discuss how AI is influencing spa operations, guest engagement, and revenue optimization. One theme surfaced repeatedly: AI creates value when it removes operational friction and gives hospitality professionals more time to focus on guests. With AI, the Future of Hospitality is More Human Hospitality has always been built on relationships, empathy, and memorable experiences. Guest expectations around personal service remain unchanged, but many teams spend significant time on administrative work that pulls them away from guest-facing responsibilities. As Jeremy McCarthy noted during the webinar, AI can automate routine tasks such as scheduling, reporting, answering common questions, and surfacing guest insights, allowing staff to focus on the moments that matter most to guests. Kelleye Martin viewed the opportunity through an operator’s lens. If AI can reduce time spent building schedules and managing administrative tasks, leaders can spend more time with guests and supporting their teams. Personalization Finally Becomes Scalable Personalization has long been a hospitality goal, but many organizations either lack sufficient guest data or collect so much information that employees struggle to identify what matters in the moment. McCarthy described this challenge as getting the right information to the right employee at the right time. The panel discussed how AI can automatically surface insights such as: Preferred therapists Treatment preferences Birthdays and anniversaries Important profile notes and guest history Martin described these details as the “golden nuggets” that help teams deliver exceptional service. Rather than searching through years of profile notes, providers can quickly see the information most relevant to an upcoming guest interaction. She also noted that spa teams often say, “the most important person is the one in front of you.” AI helps support that goal by putting relevant information at employees’ fingertips instead of requiring them to search through records while preparing for appointments. Why Unified Guest Data Matters More Than Ever One of the strongest messages from the discussion was that successful AI initiatives begin with connected guest data. Information often exists across multiple systems throughout a property. Guest preferences may live in the spa, restaurant, hotel, golf operation, or other departments. When those systems operate independently, opportunities to serve guests more effectively can be missed. When guest information is unified, teams gain a more complete view of each guest. AI can then surface insights that support a more consistent experience across the property, helping teams recognize preferences and proactively address service issues. Conversational Reservations Are Changing Expectations The panel also explored the rise of AI-powered conversational reservations. At The Houstonian, Kelleye Martin noted that call volumes can exceed 500 calls daily, with conversations frequently lasting 12 to 15 minutes, creating challenges for even well-staffed reservation teams. AI-powered voice and chat experiences can answer questions, assist with reservations, recommend upgrades, and provide information around the clock while still allowing guests to connect with a reservation specialist when needed. Martin noted that when reservation teams are fully occupied, guests may abandon calls and never call back. AI can help ensure every inquiry receives a response while still giving guests the option to speak with a person if they prefer. The Next Frontier: Revenue Optimization and Agentic AI The panel explored how future AI capabilities could help operators forecast demand, recommend staffing adjustments, identify revenue opportunities, and automate portions of operational workflows using factors such as occupancy, booking pace, weather, and historical demand patterns. The conversation also touched on agentic AI, where AI agents could coordinate tasks across systems such as filling open shifts or retrieving business insights through natural-language requests. Start Small, But Start Now Organizations do not need to transform overnight. Instead, they can start by identifying repetitive tasks where AI can provide immediate value, such as reporting, guest insight discovery, scheduling support, or reservation workflows. Kelleye Martin encouraged operators to focus on manageable use cases rather than viewing AI as an all-or-nothing decision. One example she shared was using AI to analyze reports and identify opportunities that may otherwise go unnoticed. Her advice: embrace AI where it helps your business operate more efficiently while keeping the focus on guests. As Jeremy McCarthy observed, AI is another tool that can help hospitality professionals do what they already do best. The organizations that gain the most value will likely be those that use AI to strengthen guest relationships and support the people responsible for delivering them. Related Reading: Making Hospitality More Human The webinar reinforced a simple idea: technology creates the most value when it helps people create better guest experiences. Explore how Agilysys views the role of AI, automation, and connected guest data in strengthening human hospitality in our blog, Learn More

title: Concentra Strengthens Workforce Health Access in Minnesota Through Acquisition
summary: Four Twin Cities locations join Concentra’s network, strengthening access to high-quality occupational health care DALLAS &…...
body_text: Concentra Strengthens Workforce Health Access in Minnesota Through Acquisition August 17, 2026 8:00am EDT Download as PDF Four Twin Cities locations join Concentra’s network, strengthening access to high-quality occupational health care DALLAS & MINNEAPOLIS & ST. PAUL, Minn.--(BUSINESS WIRE)-- Concentra® (NYSE: CON), the nation's leader in occupational and workforce health services, today announced completion of its acquisition of four Minnesota Occupational Health (MOH) medical centers in the Twin Cities. The acquisition strengthens access to specialized occupational health care for Minnesota employees and connects experienced local care teams with Concentra’s national clinical and operational resources. This press release features multimedia. View the full release here: https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20260817392661/en/ Beginning August 17, the medical centers will operate as Concentra, providing continuity of care for existing patients and employer customers while integrating the company’s clinical standards, technology and specialized occupational health expertise. Concentra also plans to invest in enhancing the care experience across the centers, including significant improvements to its St. Paul/Midway center that will establish it as a flagship occupational health center for the region. “Employees across Minnesota deserve access to trusted occupational health care that understands their needs and provides reliable support when and where it matters,” said Mike Kosuth, executive vice president and chief operating officer, East Group, Concentra. “By welcoming experienced local teams into Concentra’s connected network, we can expand access to specialized occupational health expertise and deliver a consistent care experience for employees across the region.” Concentra has served Minnesotans since 2018. With this acquisition, Concentra will operate eight medical centers across the state, making it easier for workers to access timely care and employers to manage workforce health across multiple locations through a consistent clinical and operational model. The acquired centers are located at: Coon Rapids – 600 Coon Rapids Boulevard NE, Suite 2, Coon Rapids, Minnesota 55433 Eagan – 1400 Corporate Center Curve, Suites 110, 120, & 200, Eagan, Minnesota 55121 St. Paul – Midway – 1661 Saint Anthony Avenue, Saint Paul, Minnesota 55104 Shakopee – 4360 12th Avenue East, Shakopee, Minnesota 55379 “Access to quality occupational health care is an important part of supporting a strong and resilient workforce,” said Mike Logan, president and CEO, MPLS Regional Chamber. “Concentra’s expanded presence in the Twin Cities gives local employers and employees greater access to specialized services that can help keep people healthy, safe, and productive. Continued investment in workforce health is good for our businesses, our employees, and the economic vitality of communities across the region.” Concentra provides a full range of occupational health services, including work injury care, physical therapy, drug testing, Department of Transportation physical exams, pre-placement exams, medical surveillance services, and workforce health programs focused on injury prevention, employee well-being, workforce readiness, and the acceleration of safe return-to-work outcomes. Telemedicine for minor work injuries will also be available through Concentra Telemed®, the company's proprietary telemedicine platform. Patients and employers can find center hours, services and more information at www.concentra.com . About Concentra Concentra is the largest provider of occupational health services in the United States by number of locations, with the mission of improving the health of America’s workforce, one patient at a time. Our approximately 13,000 colleagues and affiliated physicians and clinicians support the delivery of an extensive suite of services, including occupational and consumer health services and other direct-to-employer care. We support the care of approximately 54,000 patients each business day on average across 46 states and the District of Columbia at our 633 occupational health centers, 415 onsite health clinics at employer worksites, and Concentra Telemed as of June 30, 2026. body_text: View All News Figma Announces Second Quarter 2026 Financial Results August 5, 2026 Q2 revenue grew 48% year-over-year to $370.1 million, the third straight quarter of accelerated year-over-year growth. GAAP and non-GAAP gross profit year-over-year growth accelerated to 40%. Code Layers, the Figma agent, and new creative capabilities expand the surface for AI consumption and what teams can create in Figma. Figma raises full year revenue guidance, reflecting sustained seat expansion and AI adoption. SAN FRANCISCO--(BUSINESS WIRE)-- Figma, Inc. (NYSE:FIG) announced financial results today for its second quarter ended June 30, 2026. “Q2 was Figma’s third straight quarter of accelerated revenue growth, and as code gets commoditized and value moves up the stack, the opportunity ahead of us has only grown,” said Dylan Field, Figma's CEO. “By bringing code, new creative capabilities, and agents directly to the canvas, we’re increasing the surface for AI consumption in Figma and expanding the possibilities for what teams can create on our platform. Figma is building the canvas for full-stack creation: one place where anyone can reach for the tool they need to express their vision exactly as they imagine it.” “Q2 was a record quarter and our first full quarter of AI credit monetization,” said Praveer Melwani, Figma’s CFO. “Revenue grew 48% year-over-year, accelerating for the third consecutive quarter, and gross profit growth accelerated alongside it. Net Dollar Retention Rate remained strong at 136% as customers expanded both seats and AI credit add-ons. The strength of these signals gives us the confidence to raise our full year revenue outlook while continuing to invest behind the products we introduced at Config.” Second Quarter 2026 Financial Highlights: Revenue was $370.1 million, up 48% year-over-year and above the range of Figma’s previously issued second quarter guidance. Year-over-year revenue growth accelerated for the third sequential quarter. GAAP gross profit was $309.6 million; GAAP gross margin was 84%. Non-GAAP gross profit was $314.0 million; non-GAAP gross margin was 85%. Year-over-year growth for GAAP and non-GAAP gross profit accelerated to 40%. GAAP loss from operations was $(117.3) million; GAAP operating margin was (32)%. Non-GAAP operating income was $36.1 million; non-GAAP operating margin was 10%. GAAP and non-GAAP operating income were impacted by the increased investment in sales and marketing spend related to Figma’s annual user conference, Config. Net cash provided by operating activities was $60.9 million; operating cash flow margin was 16%. Free Cash Flow was $53.2 million; Free Cash Flow Margin was 14%. GAAP net loss was $(112.2) million and non-GAAP net income was $42.6 million. GAAP net loss per share, basic and diluted was $(0.21) and non-GAAP net income per share, basic and diluted was $0.08. Cash, cash equivalents, and marketable securities were $1.7 billion as of June 30, 2026. Recent Business & Product Highlights: Net Dollar Retention Rate was 136% as of June 30, 2026. 15,964 Paid Customers with more than $10,000 in ARR as of June 30, 2026, growing 34% year-over-year. 1,635 Paid Customers with more than $100,000 in ARR as of June 30, 2026, growing 46% year-over-year. As of June 30, 2026, over 80% of Paid Customers with more than $10,000 in ARR were consuming AI credits weekly. Hosted Config, Figma’s annual user conference, which brought over 10,000 designers, product builders, and executive leaders from the world’s leading companies to San Francisco. Announced Code Layers, which brings the power of Figma Make to the Figma design canvas. With Code Layers, teams can turn static designs into interactive, code-backed prototypes that can be edited in code or manipulated visually. Also introduced the ability for teams to work directly in their production codebase with Figma Make. Introduced new expressive capabilities on the canvas such as Motion, Shaders, and 3D Transforms; also shipped Figma Weave Tools, which turn complex AI image and video generation workflows into re-usable tools on the canvas. Together, these new capabilities expand the types of work that can happen on Figma. Launched the Figma agent, a first-party agent that’s built into the canvas, fluent in Figma, and increasingly powered by Figma’s first-party model. The Figma agent handles everything from automating repetitive tasks to generating motion animations and shaders; as of July 31, 2026, over 50% of Paid Customers with more than $10,000 in ARR were already using the Figma agent on a weekly basis. Introduced Skills, a way for teams to teach the Figma agent their own processes, governance standards, and best practices, and generative plugins, which allow teams to build custom internal tools by simply prompting the Figma agent. Third Quarter and Full Year 2026 Outlook: Based on information as of today, Figma is providing the following guidance: Third Quarter 2026 Outlook: Revenue between $373.0 million and $375.0 million, implying 36% year-over-year growth at the midpoint of the range. Full Year 2026 Outlook: Revenue between $1.463 billion and $1.467 billion, implying 39% year-over-year growth at the midpoint of the range and a raise of $40.0 million to Figma’s previously issued guidance. Non-GAAP operating income between $125.0 million and $135.0 million, representing a non-GAAP operating margin of 9% at the midpoint of the range. Conference Call Details: Figma will host a conference call today, August 5, 2026, at 5:00pm Eastern Time (2:00pm Pacific Time) to discuss its financial results for the second quarter of 2026 and outlook for the third quarter and full year 2026. Certain Definitions Figma calculates Annual Recurring Revenue (“ARR”) as the annualized value of Figma’s active customer agreements as of the measurement date, assuming any agreement that expires during the next twelve months following the measurement date is renewed on existing terms. A customer agreement is considered active when seats are provisioned to the customer at the start of their subscription. In cases where contracts are signed but not provisioned prior to the measurement date, the customer agreement is counted as active if provisioning takes place no more than 15 days after the measurement date. Figma defines a Paid Customer as a customer account that is billed separately for which Figma has an active paid subscription as of the last day of the applicable period of measurement. A single organization with multiple divisions, segments, subsidiaries, or subscribing teams that are each billed separately are counted as multiple Paid Customers. A customer account is considered active when seats are provisioned to the customer at the start of their subscription. In cases where contracts are signed but not provisioned as of the last date of the applicable period of measurement, the customer account is counted as active if provisioning takes place no more than 15 days after the last day of the applicable period of measurement. Figma defines a Paid Customer with more than $10,000 in ARR as a Paid Customer with a total of $10,000 or more of ARR as of the last day of the applicable period of measurement. Figma defines a Paid Customer with more than $100,000 in ARR as a Paid Customer with $100,000 or more of ARR as of the last day of the applicable period of measurement. Figma calculates Net Dollar Retention Rate as of the applicable period of measurement by starting with the ARR of Paid Customers with more than $10,000 in ARR as of twelve months prior to such date of measurement (“Prior Period ARR”). Figma then calculates the ARR for those same customers as of the applicable period of measurement (“Current Period ARR”). Figma then divides Current Period ARR by Prior Period ARR to calculate Net Dollar Retention Rate for the applicable date of measurement. Figma’s Net Dollar Retention Rate reflects customer expansion, contraction, and customer churn. Figma calculates Net Dollar Retention Rate using ARR from Paid Customers with more than $10,000 in ARR because Figma believes that $10,000 in ARR is an important threshold, as it is a strong indicator of significant paid usage of Figma’s products. Figma calculates Paid Customers with more than $10,000 in ARR consuming AI credits on a weekly basis for a given quarter using the week with the highest number of such users in the quarter.
